title: A rescue, a withdrawal, and the first Greek kills
intro: Idaeus escapes through divine protection. Athena then removes Ares from the battlefield, opening a sequence of Greek successes. Watch the change from dual brothers to plural armies, and the contrast between ordinary narrative and counterfactual possibility.

notes.text: ἔτλη is third singular root-aorist of τλάω, ‘endure, dare’ (compare τλῆναι). The complementary infinitive περιβῆναι is second aorist of περιβαίνω: to stand astride, here to defend his brother’s corpse. ἀδελφειοῦ is epic genitive of ἀδελφειός; κταμένοιο is genitive singular of the aorist middle participle of κτείνω, passive in sense, ‘slain.’

‘He himself would not have escaped … but Hephaestus protected him.’ κεν with the past indicative marks an unreal possibility. Homer gives the rescuing event with ἀλλά rather than expressing a complete ‘if not’ condition. ὑπέκφυγε belongs to ὑπεκφεύγω, with the aorist stem φυγ-. κῆρα is accusative of κήρ, ‘death, doom,’ not κῆρ, ‘heart.’

ἔρυτο, from ἔρυμαι, means ‘protected’; σάωσε is an unaugmented aorist of σαόω, the epic family corresponding to σῴζω. καλύψας is aorist active participle of καλύπτω: he saves him by covering him with darkness (instrumental νυκτί). ἀκαχήμενος is a perfect middle/passive participle of ἀκαχίζω, ‘grieve,’ describing a lasting distressed state.

A negative purpose clause: ‘so that the old man should not be utterly grieved.’ εἴη is optative of εἰμί after the past narrative verb; γέρων means Dares. οἱ is the third-person dative, naturally ‘his old man / priest,’ with Hephaestus in view. πάγχυ intensifies the distress, ‘altogether.’

ἐξελάσας is aorist active participle of ἐξελαύνω, ‘having driven out’ the captured horses. δῶκεν takes an infinitive of the task entrusted to the companions: ‘gave [them] to bring down to the ships.’ νῆας is accusative plural of ναῦς. υἷε is accusative dual of υἱός: the Trojans see both sons, one escaping (ἀλευάμενον, from ἀλεύομαι), the other dead.

ὄχεσφι is an epic oblique form in -φι of ὄχεα, ‘chariot,’ here after παρά with locative sense. ὀρίνθη is aorist passive of ὀρίνω, ‘stir, disturb’: their hearts were shaken. ἑλοῦσα is feminine aorist active participle of αἱρέω, from ἑλ-, ‘taking’; χειρός is the genitive of the part grasped, ‘taking him by the hand.’

ἐπέεσσι is epic dative plural of ἔπος, ‘with words.’ θοῦρος means ‘rushing, impetuous.’ Athena’s address piles up Ares’ violent titles: βροτολοιγός, ‘destroyer of mortals’; μιαιφόνος, ‘bloodstained’; τειχεσιπλήτης, ‘stormer of walls.’ τειχεσιπλῆτα is a masculine vocative in -α. The praise of violence prepares an ironic request to stop fighting.

A tactful proposal in a question: potential optative with ἄν, ‘might we not leave …?’ ἐάσαιμεν is first plural aorist active optative of ἐάω. Its accusative subjects Τρῶας and Ἀχαιούς go with μάρνασθαι, present middle infinitive of μάρναμαι, ‘fight.’ The elision in μάρνασθ᾽ hides the infinitive ending -αι.

ὁπποτέροισι is epic dative plural, ‘to whichever of the two sides.’ ὀρέξῃ is aorist active subjunctive of ὀρέγω, ‘extend, grant’; κῦδος is victorious distinction. νῶϊ is the first-person dual pronoun, ‘we two.’ χαζώμεσθα and ἀλεώμεθα are hortatory subjunctives, ‘let us withdraw’ and ‘let us avoid’; the epic -μεσθα equals -μεθα.

ἐξήγαγε is second aorist of ἐξάγω; καθεῖσεν is aorist of καθίζω, ‘seated him.’ ἠϊόεντι is dative singular of ἠϊόεις, ‘having sandy banks,’ formed from ἠϊών, ‘shore.’ ἐπί with the dative locates Ares by the river Scamander. Athena’s polite joint withdrawal results in Ares being physically parked outside the battle.

κλίνω here means ‘turn back, rout’; ἔκλιναν is aorist active. ἕλε is unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω, here ‘slew.’ ἕκαστος takes partitive ἡγεμόνων, ‘each of the leaders,’ while ἄνδρα is its distributive object, ‘a man apiece.’ Δαναοί is another collective name for the Greek army.

στρεφθέντι is aorist passive participle of στρέφω, intransitive ‘having turned’; πρώτῳ describes Odius as the first to turn. μεταφρένῳ with ἐν gives the site, ‘in the back.’ πῆξεν is an unaugmented aorist of πήγνυμι, ‘fixed, drove in.’ μεσσηγύς takes genitive ὤμων, ‘between the shoulders.’

στήθεσφιν is an epic -φι form of στῆθος, functioning with διά as ‘through the chest.’ ἔλασσε is epic aorist of ἐλαύνω, ‘drove.’ πεσών is second-aorist participle of πίπτω (ἔπεσον). δούπησεν gives the thud of the body; ἀράβησε the clatter of armour. Neuter plural τεύχεα takes a singular verb.

ἐνήρατο is aorist middle of ἐναίρω, ‘slay.’ εἰληλούθει is third singular pluperfect of ἔρχομαι: ‘had come,’ marking Phaestus’ earlier journey from Tarne. νύξε is aorist of νύσσω, ‘pierce.’ ἐπιβησόμενον is future middle participle of ἐπιβαίνω, agreeing with the victim: he was about to mount his chariot when struck.

ἤριπε is second aorist of ἐρείπω, ‘fall’; εἷλε is augmented aorist of αἱρέω, ‘seized.’ Darkness taking the warrior is a recurring death image. θεράποντες are attendants or fighting companions, here stripping the fallen man’s armour (ἐσύλευον, imperfect of συλεύω). The armour is valuable spoil as well as a sign of victory.
